chapter: Columbia and the first jazz bands
title: Kirkeby's Columbia job and the unreleased Dixieland session
summary: He was at Columbia 1914-18, in charge of test recordings, and explains how a committee chose what to record and why the Dixieland date slipped past him. He also recalls the Earl Fuller band's makeup.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: We mentioned that Earl Fuller worked for you for a time. How long were you with Columbia?
Ours was Columbia from 1914 to about 1918.
It was certainly during that time that the original New Orleans jazz band recorded at Columbia, but you don't remember it specifically.
No, that's very vague. They say that they made one date, which was not released at the time.
And it wasn't an audition record, because you were more or less in charge of that work.

I was in charge of test recording. That was new voices and new combinations that came in, you see, which we'd present to the committee, and the committee would judge them accordingly and appraise the possibilities commercially and go from there.
Well, then, they may have been engaged by the man who was in charge of all recording activities. Who was that?

Could have been. Could have been. They could have been sent on from a local dealer. There were times when artists came in to the auspices of local dealers for test recordings, which were handled by, say, the concert department or the international department, and maybe not the popular department, or maybe by one of the officials, the big officials themselves. That's how it's probably skipped by me, you see.
You would show material and suggest policy, and then somebody else would actually consult with the market people. That's right. That's right.
The committee would decide what to record.
And apparently this recording of the New Orleans jazz band wasn't brought forcefully enough to your attention until after Victor had made a success.
Yeah, yeah. You couldn't get them after that? No, that's right.
They tied up with Victor. But at that time, as I say, they started after me to get a jazz band to compete, and it was that time we...
Do you remember anybody besides Ted Lewis who was with the Earl Fuller?
Well, I think that the had... Earl Fuller, I know, played drums with the group, but who beyond that, I can't tell now.
Yeah, I think it was the original... I think it was a clarinet, which was Ted Lewis, and a trumpet, of course, and I think the usual jazz band, trombone, and the drums.
